question: What is the nominal voltage of the DA 42 NG's electrical system?
explanation: AFM 7.10.1 describes a 28 Volt DC system, subdivided into power generation, storage, distribution and consumers.

question: How many alternators does the DA 42 NG have, and what is each one's rated output?

options.text: One, rated at 140 Ampère, shared between both engines

explanation: AFM 7.10.1: power generation comes from two 70 Ampère alternators, one mounted on the bottom left side of each engine, driven by a flat belt.

question: What protects the power output line of each alternator on its way to the main bus?
explanation: AFM 7.10.1: each alternator's power line connects to its MAIN BUS via an alternator relay and a 60 Ampère circuit breaker; both main buses connect to the BATTERY BUS via a 90 Ampère breaker.

question: What circuit breaker size protects the connection between the two MAIN buses and the BATTERY BUS?
explanation: AFM 7.10.1: both LH and RH MAIN buses connect to the BATTERY BUS via a 90 Ampère circuit breaker.

question: In the event of a main battery failure, what energizes the field of each alternator?

options.text: Two 12 V, 7.2 Ah sealed lead-acid ECU backup batteries connected in series, under the passenger seats
The RH alternator's own output, cross-connected to the LH field coil
A dedicated capacitor bank in the relay junction box
External power only — the alternators cannot self-excite otherwise

explanation: AFM 7.10.1: the ECU backup batteries (two 12V 7.2Ah cells in series, under the passenger seats) energize each alternator field if the main battery fails.

question: For how long can the ECU backup batteries provide electrical power to the ECUs, under the stated condition?
explanation: AFM 7.10.1 states the ECU backup batteries provide electrical power for the ECU for a time of 30 minutes.

question: What connects each ENGINE MASTER switch to the ECU backup battery and the alternator field?
explanation: AFM 7.10.1: the ENGINE MASTER LH (RH) switch connects the ECU backup battery to the alternator field via a 10 Ampère fuse.

question: What controls the current through each alternator's field coils to keep output voltage stable across load and speed changes?

options.text: The ECU, via the fuel metering valve
The alternator control unit, via a pulse-width modulated signal

explanation: AFM 7.10.1: each alternator control unit modulates the field coil current with a pulse-width modulated signal to keep output voltage stable.

question: How do the two alternators share electrical load ("paralleling")?

options.text: The LH alternator regulator measures both alternators' outputs via separate current sensors and controls its own alternator's output accordingly
Each alternator operates completely independently with no coordination
The RH alternator regulator always takes priority over the LH regulator
Paralleling is done manually by the pilot using the VOTER switch

explanation: AFM 7.10.1: the LH alternator regulator measures both LH and RH alternator outputs and adjusts its own alternator's output to provide paralleling between them.

question: What is the capacity of the main battery?
explanation: AFM 7.10.1: the main battery is a 24 V, 13.6 Ah lead-acid battery mounted on the right-aft side of the front baggage compartment.

question: What switch controls the battery relay that connects the main battery to the BATTERY BUS?
explanation: AFM 7.10.1: the battery relay, in the relay junction box, is controlled by the ELECT. MASTER switch on the instrument panel.

question: What powers the backup attitude gyro (or standby attitude module) and the flood light in a total electrical emergency, and for how long?

options.text: The ECU backup batteries, for 30 minutes
The main 24V battery directly, for 1 hour
External power only, with no independent battery
A non-rechargeable dry emergency battery, for at least 1.5 hours when the EMERGENCY switch is set ON

explanation: AFM 7.10.1: a separate non-rechargeable dry battery supplies the standby attitude gyro/module and flood light for at least 1.5 hours when EMERGENCY is switched ON, independent of all other consumers.

question: How often must the emergency (dry) battery package be replaced?

options.text: Every 2 years, or after use (broken seal on the switch)
Every 100 flight hours regardless of use
Only when it fails a capacity test

explanation: AFM 7.10.1: the emergency battery package must be replaced every 2 years or after use (indicated by a broken seal on the EMERGENCY switch).

question: What bus is directly and permanently connected to the main battery, and cannot be disconnected from it?
explanation: AFM 7.10.1: the HOT BATTERY BUS is directly wired to the main battery and cannot be disconnected; it feeds the map/reading light and the ELT RCPI unit.

question: What does the BATTERY BUS supply heavy-duty power to, in addition to the MAIN buses?

options.text: The landing gear hydraulic pump only

explanation: AFM 7.10.1: the BATTERY BUS, reached via the battery relay, supplies the LH/RH MAIN buses and heavy-duty power to both starters.

question: What connects each ECU BUS to its MAIN BUS?

options.text: A relay switched by the AVIONIC MASTER
A fuse only, with no diode
A direct wire with no isolation component

explanation: AFM 7.10.1: the LH (RH) ECU BUS connects to its MAIN BUS via a diode, and to the alternator output via a diode and a 30 Ampère circuit breaker.

question: What size circuit breaker connects each ECU BUS to its alternator's power output line?
explanation: AFM 7.10.1: each ECU BUS connects to its alternator's power line via a diode and a 30 Ampère circuit breaker, powering ECU A and its fuel pump directly.

question: How does ECU B (and its fuel pump) receive electrical redundancy from the OPPOSITE engine's side?

options.text: Via the AVIONIC BUS, which connects both sides
Via a diode and fuse from the opposite side's ECU BUS
ECU B has no cross-side redundancy at all
Via a shared mechanical linkage to the opposite propeller governor

explanation: AFM 7.10.1: each ECU B and its fuel pump is additionally supplied from the opposite engine's ECU BUS via a diode and fuse, adding cross-side redundancy.

question: What switch must be ON to connect the RH MAIN BUS to the AVIONIC BUS?
explanation: AFM 7.10.1: the RH MAIN BUS reaches the AVIONIC BUS only via the avionics master relay, controlled by the AVIONIC MASTER switch.

question: Under normal operating conditions, what voltage does the voltmeter display?

options.text: The main battery voltage at all times
An average of both alternators and the battery

explanation: AFM 7.10.1: under normal conditions the voltmeter shows alternator voltage; otherwise it displays main battery voltage.

question: What does the ammeter display?

options.text: The current supplied to the electrical system by the LH (RH) alternator
The total current drawn by all avionics combined
The current flowing through the ECU backup batteries only
The starter motor current during engine start

explanation: AFM 7.10.1: the ammeter for each side shows the current supplied to the electrical system by that side's alternator.

question: What protects the external power socket from reverse polarity?
explanation: AFM 7.10.1: a diode in the external power socket circuit protects the system from reverse polarity.

question: How many ECUs control each engine, and what is the role of the VOTER switch when set to AUTO?

options.text: Two ECUs, with AUTO always favoring ECU A
Three ECUs, with AUTO cycling between them every flight
Two ECUs (A and B) per engine; AUTO lets the system propose the better-performing or lower-hours ECU automatically
One ECU per engine, with the VOTER only used for maintenance testing

explanation: AFM 7.10.2: the electronic ECU consists of two ECUs per engine; a VOTER switch set to AUTO proposes an ECU based on operating hours or, after a failure, better engine control capability.

question: If the VOTER switch is manually set to A or B instead of AUTO, what happens?

options.text: The engine shuts down for safety
Nothing changes; VOTER position only affects indications
The corresponding ECU is forced to control the engine

explanation: AFM 7.10.2: setting VOTER to A or B forces that specific ECU to control the engine, rather than letting the system choose automatically.

question: What is the difference between a "latched" and a "non-latched" ECU fault indication?

options.text: A latched fault requires unscheduled maintenance and remains until cleared by maintenance; a non-latched fault clears itself once its cause is gone
A latched fault clears itself after landing; a non-latched fault requires maintenance
Both types always require maintenance, differing only in urgency
A non-latched fault can never be cleared in flight, unlike a latched one

explanation: AFM 7.10.2: a latched caution needs unscheduled maintenance and notifying Austro Engine; a non-latched caution disappears once its cause is no longer present.

question: How many crew-alerting levels does the G1000 CAS use?

options.text: Five, matching the five engine parameter arcs
Four: Warning, Caution, Advisory, and Informational

explanation: AFM 7.10.3 describes three alert levels: Warning (red), Caution (amber), and Advisory (white).

question: What does pressing the MSG key do when no master alert is currently active?

options.text: Switches the display to reversionary (composite) mode
Opens a pop-up auxiliary flight display page listing all active alerts
Silences all future aural alerts for the remainder of the flight

explanation: AFM 7.10.3: pressing MSG with no new alert active opens the pop-up AFD page, which lists every currently active alert regardless of level.
